title: Describe the story as a visible action or reveal
instruction: Express the article connection through a recognizable scene with a visible action, relationship, or reveal. Name what the viewer should notice and why; avoid relying on an inventory of symbolic objects to communicate the story.

evidence.excerpt:
A superbly equipped raven archer has everything needed to succeed—specialized optics, an excellent bow, carefully prepared arrows—but has still missed the actual goal. The visual metaphor is “good tools and support do not guarantee the right outcome.”

Show this through one immediately readable scene, not a diagram: a confident, well-equipped raven on the left, facing a tilted archery target on the right. Three previously fired arrows have struck the target well away from its untouched bullseye.

The irony should come from the contrast between the archer’s impressive equipment and the conspicuously poor results. Do not make the raven look foolish, confused, or incompetent.

STYLE AND MATERIALS
Layered cut-paper still life, photographed as a clean editorial studio image. Every element—including the raven, its equipment, the arrows, and the target—is constructed from matte cut paper.

CONCEPT
A beautiful, impressive house front turns out to be only a freestanding façade, held up from behind by a single ordinary 2×4. The story is the contrast between a polished, substantial-looking exterior and its surprisingly makeshift support. The attractive house should draw the viewer in; the exposed thin edge and diagonal brace should reveal the illusion immediately afterward.

title: Specify role, posture, gaze, and grip independently
instruction: Specify the character role and costume, torso orientation, head angle, gaze target, and how held objects are supported. Distinguish the object being held from the object receiving attention when they differ.

evidence.excerpt:
Give both the car and the testing operation substantial visual presence. The main subjects occupy roughly three quarters of the canvas, with clean breathing room around their silhouettes; secondary workshop furniture may extend toward the edges. Keep the raven’s inspection sheet, the copper adjustment handle, the sensor-to-car relationship, and the car’s wheels around the central band so a wide thumbnail crop retains the story.

RAVEN MECHANIC
Match the approved raven character: charcoal layered feather shapes, substantial slate-teal beak, off-white eyes with dark pupils, compact body, tapered tail, slender bird legs and toes, and wings that can grip objects through feather-like fingers.

Dress the raven as a modern Formula 1 team mechanic, not in an apron. Give it a fitted charcoal technical mechanic’s jumpsuit with light-gray inset panels, narrow burnt-copper stripes along the outer sleeves and trouser legs, practical seams, a simple belt, and one small utility pocket containing a wrench and an orange-handled tool. All clothing is made from layered matte paper. No branding, team names, sponsor patches, lettering, or helmet. Keep the feathered head, neck, wing tips, tail, and bird feet visible.

Show the raven in a three-quarter rear/side view, with its shoulders turned toward the wall monitors and its head tilted upward to study the middle screen. Keep the recognizable eye and beak visible in profile. Its gaze must clearly meet the monitor graphics rather than the car or the sheet in its wings.

The raven holds a large off-white inspection printout below its face, around chest-to-waist height, with feather-like fingers supporting the edges. Include only a small car silhouette, an illustrative line graph, broad document blocks, and a wheel diagram. The printout supports its comparison with the electronic results, but its attention is currently on the monitors. Its posture is attentive, analytical, and composed.

title: Spell out physical connections and movement
instruction: Describe what connects to what, where the support or attachment meets its object, and which direction material moves. Specify physically important differences between stages so the process reads without explanatory arrows.

evidence.excerpt:
The cards are blank, mostly rectangular or square, with subtly irregular hand-cut edges. Include three visibly distinct sizes: large cards, medium cards, and tiny pieces. Use off-white, pale sage, and deep slate teal for the cards.

Print “All the News” clearly on the bucket’s visible side.

FIRST STAGE — “Big Stories”
Below and to the right of the input bucket is a broad, shallow, deep-slate-teal sieve-container. Its elliptical opening reveals a perforated base with large, clearly visible circular holes.

The sieve and collection container are one integrated object, not separate objects stacked together. Its front paper sidewall is labeled “Big Stories.”

Several large cards remain visibly inside, too large to pass through the holes. Medium and small cards fall out through its bottom onto the first conveyor belt directly below it.

FIRST CONVEYOR
A simple horizontal matte-paper belt loop carries the medium and small cards to the right.

Construct the belt from a dark paper band around two simple circular paper rollers. No motor, gears, legs, framework, or elaborate machinery.

Its left portion sits beneath the Big Stories sieve. Its right end finishes above the opening of the next container, allowing the cards to visibly tumble off the belt into it. The receiving container must sit lower; the cards should never need to travel uphill.

SECOND STAGE — “Medium Reads”
Lower and farther right is a pale-sage sieve-container with the same shallow, folded-paper construction. Label its front sidewall “Medium Reads.”

Its perforated base has noticeably smaller, more densely spaced circular holes than the Big Stories sieve.

Medium cards remain visibly inside. Only the tiny pieces pass through its bottom, falling onto a second conveyor belt below.

SECOND CONVEYOR
A second simple horizontal matte-paper belt loop carries only tiny paper pieces toward the lower right.

Use the same restrained construction as the first conveyor: one dark paper belt and two circular paper rollers.

Place this belt distinctly lower than the first. Its right end finishes above the final bucket’s opening, with a short visible stream of tiny pieces falling into that bucket.

FAÇADE CONSTRUCTION AND SUPPORT
This is only the decorated front wall of a house, like a theatrical stage flat. There is no enclosed building behind it, no full side wall, and no deep roof structure. The roofline and chimney belong to the same shallow, layered silhouette.

Show the narrow exposed cardstock edge along the left side so the viewer can clearly understand how thin the façade is. Let the whole panel lean very slightly backward toward its support—not enough to look like it is falling, but enough to suggest that the brace is necessary.

One straight, narrow, rectangular 2×4 extends diagonally from the ground at the lower left to a point roughly halfway up the back of the façade. Its upper end disappears behind the left edge of the house. Make the connection physically convincing: the timber is visibly propping up the panel, not lying beside it or passing across its decorated front. A small simple foot block is acceptable, but do not add another brace, scaffolding, or a substantial support frame.

Render the 2×4 in burnt-copper paper, with only a subtle lengthwise edge or seam to suggest its rectangular timber form.

The car is stationary on a robust charcoal dynamometer-style test stand. Clearly show the tires resting between cylindrical rollers. Include substantial beams, triangular braces, visible paper-cut bolts, roller axles, and sturdy supports. Burnt-copper wheel restraints with charcoal brackets secure the visible front and rear wheels to the rig. Make the physical connection between car, rollers, restraints, and support frame unmistakable.

Retain a prominent burnt-copper adjustment handwheel with a short projecting grip on the upright near the car’s front-left corner. It belongs to the testing apparatus, not to the car.

LIVE TESTING MONITORS
Replace wall-mounted paper charts with exactly three modern flat-panel computer monitors in simple charcoal frames above the rear workbench. Their displays represent results from the roadster’s ongoing test.

Left monitor: a side-profile roadster silhouette, broad horizontal readout bars, and a small wheel diagram.
Middle monitor: two semicircular gauge arcs above a simple graph with teal and copper curves, plus a few vertical indicator bars.
Right monitor: a waveform plot beside an overhead axle-and-wheel schematic, with a few small status dots and abstract readout blocks.

Use layered paper lines and shapes for every interface element. The graphics are schematic visual shorthand, not real statistics or evidence. No words, numerals, scores, checkmarks, or pass/fail verdicts. Avoid neon, screen bloom, holograms, or colored light spilling onto the workshop.

ELECTRONIC TESTING APPARATUS
Make the sensors visibly contemporary and electronic, rather than a simple mechanical measuring arm. A sturdy vertical mast attached to the rig supports an articulated assembly of compact rectangular sensor housings, adjustment joints, and a precise measuring head positioned just above the roadster’s front bodywork.

Add a second compact sensor module near the rear wheel, mounted on its own support and aimed toward the vehicle. Connect the modules to the rig with a few neatly routed black cables, small copper connectors, and one short coiled lead. Include a compact control or acquisition box attached to the test stand and a single thicker conduit exiting the rig.

Use small matte indicator dots and simple panel details without text. Keep the electronics believable and orderly, with clear mounting points and purposeful connections. No floating devices, glowing scanning beams, or decorative circuitry.

instruction: State the intended scene state and exclude plausible but misleading endings. A candidate still under evaluation should remain visibly restrained or awaiting judgment; avoid success verdicts or release cues unless the selected concept requires them.
